France (a country located primarily in Western Europe)

mi.etymology: From Latin mē, and possibly, as an indirect object, in part from Latin mihi.

love.etymology: From Latin lupa, feminine of lupus. Compare Venetan lova, French louve.

glosses_en: Portugal (a country in Southern Europe, on the Iberian Peninsula)

see.etymology: From the verb seâ. Compare Italian sega, Venetan siega, French scie.

at.etymology: From Latin actus. Cognate with Italian atto.

vert.etymology: From Late Latin virdis, syncopated from Latin viridis. Compare Italian verde.

face.etymology: From Late Latin facia, from Latin faciēs (“face, shape”).

re.etymology: From Latin rēx, rēgem. Compare Italian re.

torte.etymology: From Latin turta. Thought to derive from Latin tŏrta f (“twisted”), but this is phonologically problematic (cf. Friulian tuart < Latin tŏrtus).

dove.etymology: From Latin doga, from Ancient Greek δοχή (dokhḗ), from Proto-Indo-European *doḱ-éh₂. Compare Italian doga, Venetan dova, doa, French douve.

let.etymology: Inherited from Latin lēctus, perfect passive participle of legō.

sot.etymology: From Latin subtus, which is derived from Latin sub. Cognate to Ladin sot, Romansh sut, suot, Venetan sóto, Italian sotto, French sous, Romanian sub, supt.

none.etymology: Feminine of nono. Compare Italian nonna, Venetan nona.

glosses_en: Europe (a continent located west of Asia and north of Africa)

bo.etymology: From Latin bōs, bōvem, probably through Vulgar Latin *boem.

anime.etymology: From Latin anima (“breath, soul”) (cf. Italian alma, Romansh olma).

lune.etymology: From Latin lūna, from Proto-Italic *louksnā, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂.

ti.etymology: Inherited from Latin tē, accusative singular of tū. As an indirect object, in part from Latin tibi, dative singular of tū, through a Vulgar Latin *ti.

ce.etymology: From Latin quid. Compare Italian che, Venetan ché, Romanian ce.

lu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *illu, from Latin illum. Compare Italian lo.

spade.etymology: From Latin spatha (“a type of sword”), from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “broad blade”).

glosses_en: Tuscany (an administrative region of Italy, located north of Lazio and south of Emilia-Romagna)

net.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *nittus, from Latin nitidus.

Rome, Ancient Rome (an ancient empire based out of the city of Rome, covering vast territories in Europe, Asia and Africa; in full, Roman Empire)

cent.etymology: From Latin centum, from Proto-Italic *kəntom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm.

front.etymology: From Latin frontem, accusative singular of frōns.

code.etymology: From Vulgar Latin cōda, variant of Latin cauda.

glosses_en: Malta (an archipelago and country in Southern Europe, in the Mediterranean Sea)
Malta (the largest island in the Maltese Archipelago)

ton.etymology: From Latin tonus, from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos). Compare Italian tuono, Romansh tun, tung, Dalmatian tun, Romanian tun.

rude.etymology: From Latin rūta, from Ancient Greek ῥυτή (rhutḗ).

desert.etymology: From Latin dēsertum (in this form possibly a semi-learned term; cf. the variant form).

arme.etymology: From Late Latin arma (“weapon”), from Latin arma (“defensive arms”).

chest.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *eccum iste (see there for cognates), from Latin eccum (“behold”) + iste (“that”). Compare Ladin chest and Romansh quest.

bos.etymology: From Latin buxus, from Ancient Greek πύξος (púxos).

glosses_en: Mongolia (a Mongolian-speaking geographic region in East Asia, including the country of Mongolia (Outer Mongolia), the autonomous region of Inner Mongolia in China, and sometimes also Buryatia, Tuva and the Altai Republic in Russia)
Asia (the largest continent, located between Europe and the Pacific Ocean)

barbe.etymology: From Latin barba, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰeh₂.

stale.etymology: Of Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *stallaz. Compare Romansh stalla, stala, Italian stalla, Venetan stała.

glosses_en: Naples (a port city and comune, the capital of the Metropolitan City of Naples and the region of Campania, Italy)
Naples (a metropolitan city of Campania, established in 2015; in full, the Metropolitan City of Naples)

gland.etymology: From Latin glāndem, accusative of glāns.

nono.etymology: Compare Italian nonno, Venetan nono. Ultimately from Latin nonnus.

dis-.etymology: From Latin dis-, from Proto-Indo-European *dwís. See also s-.

program.etymology: From Late Latin programma (“a proclamation, edict”), from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma, “a written public notice, an edict”).

passare.etymology: From Latin passer, passerem. Compare Italian passero, Romansh pasler, Romanian pasăre, French passereau, Spanish pájaro.

tei.etymology: From Latin tilia, changed into a masculine. Compare Italian tiglio, Romanian tei, Catalan tell.

il.etymology: From Latin illum, ultimately from ille.

lis.etymology: From Latin illas, accusative feminine plural of illae.

blanc.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin blancus.

glace.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *glacium/a, from Latin glaciēs.

trist.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin trīstus, from Latin trīstis. Compare Italian tristo.

artist.etymology: From Late Latin artista (“artist”), from ars (“art”).

za.etymology: From Latin iam. Compare Italian già.

glosses_en: apocopic form of il, la: the

côr.etymology: From Latin chorus, from Ancient Greek χορός (khorós, “dance, chorus, choir”).

jo.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin eo, from Classical Latin egō̆.

dint.etymology: From Latin dēns, dentem. Compare Italian dente, Romansh dent, Venetan dénte, Romanian dinte, French dent, Spanish diente.

ream.etymology: Probably from Latin regimen, regimine. Compare French royaume (Old French reaume, reiame), Occitan reialme, Romansh reginam.

dean.etymology: From Late Latin decānus, from Latin decem (“ten”). Compare Italian decano, Venetan degàn, French doyen.

lame.etymology: Ultimately from Latin lāmina. Compare Romansh loma, lama, French lame, Italian and Venetan lama.

raze.etymology: Uncertain; possibly of South Slavic or substrate origin. Compare Slovene raca, Romanian rață.

sut.etymology: From Latin exsūctus (compare Ladin sut, Venetan suto, Dalmatian sot, Italian asciutto, Sicilian (a)sciuttu), or less likely sūctus (compare Romanian supt).

von.etymology: Probably ultimately from a derivative of Latin avus, or a related term, possibly a diminutive. Compare Italian avo, avolo. Cf. also archaic Romanian bun (“grandfather”) (modern bunic), Calabrian Sicilian and Piedmontese bona (“grandmother”)

verge.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *virdia (see for cognates), from syncopation of Latin viridia, neuter plural of viridis (“green”).

gust.etymology: From Latin gustus, from Proto-Italic *gustus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus. Possibly a borrowing or semi-learned term.

bati.etymology: From Latin battere, from earlier battuere.

cope.etymology: From Late Latin cuppa, from Latin cūpa.

puint.etymology: From Latin pontem, singular accusative of pōns.

trai.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *tragere, from Latin trahere.

fie.etymology: From Latin fīlia. Compare Italian and Romansch figlia, Romanian fie, French fille.

Lui.etymology: From Latin iūlius, through dissimilation. Compare Romansh lügl, Venetan lujo, Italian luglio.

glosses_en: mine; the thing belonging to me

cali.etymology: From Vulgar Latin, Late Latin quāglum/ *coāglum, from Latin coāgulum. See also the borrowing coagul.

glosses_en: Catalan, Catalonian (of, from or relating to Catalonia, Spain)

lint.etymology: From Latin lēns, lentem. Compare Italian and Venetan lente, lent, Romanian linte.

fari.etymology: From Latin fabrum, accusative of faber.

ridi.etymology: From Late Latin rīdere, from Latin rīdēre (“laugh”).

voli.etymology: From Vulgar Latin oclus, from Latin oculus.

movi.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *movĕre, from Latin movēre.

savon.etymology: From Latin sāpōnem, accusative singular of sāpō (“soap”), from Proto-Germanic *saipǭ (“soap”).

menace.etymology: From Latin minācia (“threat”), possibly via Italian minaccia or another Romance language.

ete.etymology: Ultimately from Latin aetās, aetātem. Cf. Italian età.

lat.etymology: From Late Latin lactem, from Latin lac.

lunis.etymology: From Latin Lūnae diēs, variant of diēs Lūnae (“day of the moon”).

tos.etymology: From Latin tussis, tussem, from Proto-Italic *tussis, from Proto-Indo-European *tud-ti-s (“cough”), from *(s)tewd-, from *(s)tew- (“to push, hit”).

rognon.etymology: Compare Italian rognone, French rognon. Derived (possibly indirectly) from a Vulgar Latin *rēniō, *rēniōnem, from Latin rēn (“kidney”).

doi.etymology: From Latin duo. Compare Ladin doi, Italian due, Dalmatian doi, Romanian doi, French deux, Spanish dos.

glosses_en: Lombardy (an administrative region in northern Italy, where its capital and the largest city Milan is founded in the Po Valley)

dut.etymology: From Vulgar Latin tōttus, alteration of Latin tōtus. Compare Ladin dut, Romansh tut, Istriot doûto, Italian tutto, Romanian tot, French tout, Spanish todo.

ment.etymology: From Latin mentem, accusative singular of mēns (“mind”), from Proto-Indo-European *méntis.

len.etymology: From Latin lignum. Compare Ladin lën, Romansh len, lenn, lain.

felet.etymology: From Latin filictum (“place abounding in ferns”) (compare Spanish helecho (“fern”), Corsican filetta), from filix (“fern”).

montagne.etymology: Probably borrowed from Italian montagna, from Early Medieval Latin montānia, a collective based on Latin montem.

mont.etymology: From Latin montem, accusative of mōns.

sere.etymology: From Late Latin sēra, from ellipsis of Latin sēra diēs, from sērus (“late”). Compare Italian sera, Venetan séra, Romansh saira, seira, Romanian seară, French soir.

mei.etymology: From Latin milium. Compare Italian miglio, Venetan méjo, Romanian mei, Dalmatian mail, Catalan mill, Spanish mijo.

glosses_en: mine; the thing belonging to me

vierte.etymology: From the feminine of viert, past participle of vierzi (“to open”). Compare Venetan verta.

ardi.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ārdĕre, from Latin ārdēre.

aur.etymology: From Latin aurum. Compare Romansh aur, Venetan oro, Italian oro, Dalmatian jaur, Romanian aur, French or.

vot.etymology: From Latin octō. Compare Catalan vuit.

mulin.etymology: From Late Latin molīnum, from molīnus, from Latin molō.

nore.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *nŏra, from Late Latin nura, from Classical Latin nurus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *snusós.

glosses_en: Aragon (a medieval kingdom, now an autonomous community, in northeastern Spain)

balcon.etymology: Of Germanic origin; possibly from Lombardic balko (“beam”), from Proto-Germanic *balkô (“beam”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵ- (“beam, pile, prop”). Compare Venetan balcon.

glosses_en: Estonia (a country in northeastern Europe, on the southeastern coast of the Baltic Sea)

zun.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin derivative of Latin jejūnus, from ieiūnus.

glosses_en: Australia (a country consisting of a main island, the island of Tasmania and other smaller islands, located in Oceania; historically, a collection of former colonies of the British Empire)
Australia (a continent consisting of the land on the Australian tectonic plate, i.e. Australia, New Guinea and intervening islands)

medem.etymology: Probably from Vulgar Latin *metipsimus, from Latin -met + ipse + -issimus. Compare Ladin medemo, Romansh medem, madem, Italian medesimo, Venetan medemo, medesino, Lombard medemm, Piedmontese midem, Romagnol medësum, French même, Portuguese

timp.etymology: From Latin tempus, from Proto-Indo-European *tempos (“stretch”), from the root *temp- (“to stretch, string”).

bosc.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin boscus, borrowed from Frankish *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz.

glosses_en: Serbia (a country on the Balkan Peninsula in Southeastern Europe)
Somalia (a country in East Africa, in the Horn of Africa)

corone.etymology: From Latin corōna, from Ancient Greek κορώνη (korṓnē).

doman.etymology: From Late Latin dē māne (“early in the morning”). Compare Ladino doman, Romansh damaun.

duche.etymology: Ultimately from Latin dux, ducem, borrowed or through the intermediate of another language, probably Italian duca. Compare also the doublet dûs.

mondan.etymology: From Late Latin mundānus. Compare French mondain.

velen.etymology: From Latin venēnum. Compare Italian veleno.

glosses_en: Provence (a maritime geographic region and former province of southeastern France bordering Italy; since 2016 included in the administrative region of Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur)

soe.etymology:
From Vulgar Latin, Late Latin soca, of Celtic origin, from Gaulish *soucā, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sew- (“to bend, to cut, to drive”), see also Sanskrit सुवति (suvati).

spese.etymology: From Late Latin expe(n)sa, from Latin expensus, from expendere. Compare Ladin speisa, Romansh spaisa, Venetan spexa, Italian spesa, Old French espoise.

jù.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin iūsum, from Classical Latin deorsum.

messe.etymology: From Late Latin missa, from Latin missum.

diaul.etymology: From Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin diabolus (possibly semi-learned), from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos).

canibal.etymology: From Spanish caníbal, from Taíno caniba.

mîl.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *melem m or f, from Latin mel n.

stope.etymology: From Latin stuppa, from Ancient Greek στύππη (stúppē).

albe.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *alba, from Latin albus. Compare Italian alba.

fumate.etymology: From the feminine past participle of fumâ (“to smoke”). Compare French fumée.

fenoli.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *fenuclum, from Late Latin fēnuculum, a diminutive of Latin fēnum.

verze.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *virdia, contraction of Latin viridia. Compare Italian verza, Portuguese verça, Spanish berza, Romanian varză.

fontane.etymology: From Late Latin fontāna, from substantivation of the adjective Latin fontānus, from fons.

magri.etymology: From Latin macrum, accusative singular of macer.

strade.etymology: From Late Latin strāta (“paved road”), from Latin [via] strāta, feminine of strātus.

lote.etymology: From Late Latin lucta, from Latin luctor.

teren.etymology: From Latin terrēnum. Cf. Italian terreno.

semence.etymology: From Late Latin sementia, plural of sementium, neuter form derived from Latin sēmentis, itself derived from sēmen (“seed”). Compare Venetan semensa.

cuc.etymology: From Late Latin cucus or cuccus, compare also Latin cuculus.

glosses_en: Tasmania (an island group and state of Australia; a former British colony, from 1856 to 1901)

rogne.etymology: From Latin arānea, possibly through a Vulgar Latin root *ronea or *aronea, influenced by rodō (“gnaw”). Compare Italian rogna.

frece.etymology: From Italian freccia, from Vulgar Latin *fleccia.

braç.etymology: From Latin brachium, bracchium, from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn).

piere.etymology: From Latin petra, from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra).

viru.etymology: From a derivative of Latin verres.

citât.etymology: From Derived from Late Latin cīvitātem (“city”).

frut.etymology: From Latin frūctus (“produce, product, yield; enjoyment; effect”).

vues.etymology: From Latin ossum, popular variant of os. Compare Romansh ies, oss, Venetan oso, Italian osso, Dalmatian vuas, Istriot uosso.

fiât.etymology: From Late Latin fīcātum (“liver”), from Latin iecur fīcātum (“fig-stuffed liver”).

olme.etymology: Compare Italian orma, Venetan usma, Istriot urma, Romanian urmă.

predi.etymology: From Vulgar Latin previter, from Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros).

taule.etymology: Ultimately from Latin tabula. Compare Italian tavola, Venetan toła, Occitan and Catalan taula.

cueste.etymology: From Latin costa. Compare Italian costa, Romansh costa, Dalmatian cuasta, Romanian coastă, French côte, Spanish cuesta.

istorie.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin historia, from Ancient Greek ἱστορίᾱ (historíā).

zardìn.etymology: From French jardin (compare Italian giardino, Spanish jardín), from Middle French jardin, from Old French jardin (“garden, enclosure”), probably from Vulgar Latin or early Gallo-Romance [hortus] gardinus, from Frankish *gardin, oblique case

nibli.etymology: From Late Latin nibulus, from an alteration of Latin milvus.

pome.etymology: From Latin pōma, plural of pōmum, interpreted as a feminine singular.

viert.etymology: Variant of aviert, from Latin apertus. Compare Venetan verto.

ric.etymology: Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz. Compare Italian ricco.

sience.etymology: From Latin scientia, probably a semi-learned borrowing. Compare Italian scienza, French science.

dulie.etymology: From dulî, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *dolia, from Latin dolor. Compare Italian doglia.

strie.etymology: From Latin strīga, from strīx, from Ancient Greek στρίξ (stríx). Compare Romansh stria, streia, Ladin stria, Italian strega, Venetan striga, Lombard stria, Old French estrie, Romanian strigă.

glosses_en: Liguria (an administrative region of northwest Italy)

tenar.etymology: From Latin tener, tenerum. Compare Romansh tener, tegnair, Italian tenero, French tendre, Romanian tânăr.

dret.etymology: From Late Latin drictus, from Latin dīrēctus.

tenture.etymology: From Latin tinctūra, future active participle of tingō (“to moisten”).

sanc.etymology: From Vulgar Latin sanguem, alteration of Latin sanguinem, accusative of sanguis.

mitât.etymology: From Late Latin medietātem, accusative of medietās, from Latin medius.

chel.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *(ec)cu illu, contracted from the accusative of Vulgar Latin *eccum ille.

glosses_en: Prussia (a geographical area on the Baltic coast of Northeast Europe)
Prussia (a former duchy, kingdom and (after German unification in 1871) a federal state of Germany, existing from 1525 to 1947, mostly in areas now part of Germany, Poland and Russia)

friture.etymology: From frit + -ure, or possibly a Vulgar Latin *frīctūra, from Latin frīctus. Compare French friture, Italian frittura, Romanian friptură, Spanish and Portuguese fritura.

spi.etymology: From Latin spīcum, alternative form of spīca. Compare French épi, Italian spiga, Romanian spic.

moviment.etymology: From movi + -ment, or perhaps partly based on Medieval Latin mōvimentum, from Latin moveō.

vintri.etymology: From Latin venter. Compare Italian ventre, Romansh venter, Romanian vintre, French ventre.

batel.etymology: Related to bati; from a derivative of Latin battuō, battuere, cf. Vulgar Latin *bataclum < *bat(t)uaculum. Compare French batail, Catalan batall, Italian battaglio. See also batecul.

preiere.etymology: From Old French preiere, from Early Medieval Latin precāria, derived from Latin precem.

verd.etymology: From Late Latin virdis, syncopated from Latin viridis. Compare Italian verde.

tinde.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin or Late Latin tenda, from Vulgar Latin *tendita, substantivized feminine of *tenditus, as a variant form of tentus, perfect passive participle of Latin tendō. Compare Italian tenda, Portuguese tenda, Spanish tienda

stes.etymology:
From Vulgar Latin *(i)stipsum, a contracted form of Latin
istum (“that, particular”) + ipsum (“himself”). Compare Ladin stes, Romansh listess, Venetan steso, stes, Italian stesso.

palment.etymology: From Latin pavīmentum. Compare Old Italian palmiento (modern pavimento), Romanian pământ.

mascli.etymology: From Vulgar Latin masclus, from Latin masculus.

palmon.etymology: From Latin pulmōnem, accusative singular of pulmō.

mêl.etymology: From Late Latin mēlum, from Latin mālum. Compare Romansh mail, Romanian măr.

esam.etymology: Borrowed from Latin exāmen. Compare scuam.

poete.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin poēta, from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs, “creator, maker, author, poet”).

cusin.etymology: Compare Italian cugino, French cousin. Ultimately from Latin cōnsobrīnus, possibly through the French or Italian intermediate.

parè.etymology: From parê. Compare Italian parere, Romanian părere.

bagn.etymology: Inherited from Latin baneum, variant of balneum.

glosses_en: Andalusia (a historical region and autonomous community in southern Spain, the most populated and second largest of the seventeen autonomous communities that constitute Spain)

nazion.etymology: From Latin nātiōnem, likely via Italian nazione.

mirinde.etymology: From Latin merenda. Compare Italian merenda, Romanian merinde, Spanish merienda.

glosses_en: patch (of cloth or leather used in mending)

alc.etymology: From Latin aliquod. Compare Spanish algo.

capele.etymology: From Medieval Latin, from Late Latin cappella, from the diminutive of cappa; probably a borrowing or through Italian cappella.

dêt.etymology: From Latin digitus (“finger”), from Proto-Indo-European *diǵ-, zero-grade of *deyǵ- (“to show, point out, pronounce solemnly”).

ìsule.etymology: From Latin īnsula (“island”) (compare French île, Italian isola, Spanish isla).

spieli.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *speclum, from Latin speculum.

starnudade.etymology: From the feminine past participle of starnudâ. Compare Venetan starnudada.

vogade.etymology: From the feminine past participle of vogâ. Compare Venetan vogada, Italian vogata.

pareli.etymology: From Late Latin pariculus, diminutive of Latin pār. Compare Italian parecchio.

nole.etymology: Inherited from Latin nucula. Compare Italian nocchia and nocciola, Venetan noxeła, Romansh nitschola, Sicilian nuzzola, Franco-Provençal nusèlye, Occitan nosilha; cf. also French noisette.

glosses_en: Arabia (a peninsula of West Asia between the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf; includes Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Oman, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, and the United Arab Emirates)
Arabia (the region of West Asia within or adjacent to the Arabian Plate; Yemen, Oman, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, the Egyptian Sinai, Palestine and the United Arab Emirates)

popul.etymology: Borrowed from Italian popolo, from Latin populus.

spale.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *spatla, from Late Latin spatula, diminutive of Latin spatha (“straight sword”).

glosses_en: reef, cliff or rock in the sea
scoi.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *scoculum, from Latin scopulus, from Ancient Greek.

cuar.etymology: From Latin cornū. Compare Italian corno, Dalmatian cuarno, Spanish cuerno.

pugn.etymology: From Latin pugnus. Compare Romansh pugn, Italian pugno.

glosses_en: Armenia (a country in the South Caucasus region of Asia, sometimes considered to belong politically to Europe)

fuart.etymology: From Latin fortis, fortem. Compare Italian forte, Dalmatian fuart, Romanian foarte, Spanish fuerte, French and Catalan fort.

muart.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *mortu(s), from Latin mortuus. Compare Italian morto, Dalmatian muart, Romansh miert, Venetan morto, Romanian mort, Spanish muerto, French and Catalan mort.

lâ.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin alāre.

coion.etymology: From Late Latin cōleōnem, derived from Latin cōleus (“sack, scrotum”). Compare Venetan cojon.

glosses_en: Piedmont (an administrative region in the north of Italy)

parint.etymology: From Latin parentem, accusative singular of parēns.

vescul.etymology: From Late Latin episcopus (“overseer, bishop”) (compare Italian vescovo), from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “overseer”).

ànime.etymology: From Latin anima (“breath, soul”) (compare Italian alma, Romansh olma, Venetan ànema).

gjat.etymology: From Late Latin cattus. Compare Romansh giat.

vissie.etymology: From Latin vessīca, variant of vēsīca.

regjon.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin regiō, regiōnem.

sufrî.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *sufferīre, from Latin sufferre.

strent.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *strinctus, from Latin strictus. Compare old Italian and Neapolitan strinto, Venetan strento, Romanian strâmt, Logudorese Sardinian istrintu, French étreint.

misurâ.etymology: From Late Latin mēnsūrāre, from Latin mēnsūra.

lusî.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *lūcīre, from Latin lūcēre.

svolâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *exvolāre, from Latin ex- + volāre. Compare Romansh svolar.

scuarce.etymology: From Latin scortea, feminine noun form of scorteus (“made of skin or leather”).

vuere.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin werra, borrowed from Frankish *werʀu (“confusion; quarrel”).

buine sere.etymology: buine + sere. Compare Italian buona sera, French bonsoir, Romanian bună seară.

sutiliâ.etymology: From Late Latin subtīliāre, from Latin subtīlis.

puarte.etymology: From Latin porta. Compare Italian porta, Romansh porta, Dalmatian puarta, Istriot puorta, Romanian poartă, Spanish puerta, French porte.

scuele.etymology: From Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ). Compare Italian scuola, Spanish escuela.

blestemâ.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin blastēmāre (variant of blasphēmāre).

guviêr.etymology: From the verb guviernâ. Compare Ladin guviern, Italian governo, Catalan govern, Spanish gobierno, Portuguese governo, French gouvernement.

guviernâ.etymology: From Latin gubernāre, from Ancient Greek κυβερνάω (kubernáō).

mierli.etymology: From Late Latin merŭlum, from Latin merula.

sigûr.etymology: From Latin sēcūrus. Compare Venetan seguro, siguro, Italian sicuro, Catalan segur.

sengul.etymology: From Latin singulus. Compare Italian singolo, Romanian singur.

ruzin.etymology: From Latin aerūgō, aerūginem (“copper rust”). Compare Italian ruggine, Romanian rugină.

fiêr.etymology: From Latin ferrum. Compare Romansh fier, Romanian fier, Dalmatian fiar, Italian ferro, French fer, Spanish hierro.

ferbint.etymology: From Latin fervēns, fervēntem. Compare Romanian fierbinte.

fevelâ.etymology: From Late Latin fābellārī, a verb based on Latin fābella, the diminutive of fābula (“narrative; story”).

cuarde.etymology: From Latin chorda, from Ancient Greek χορδή (khordḗ, “string of gut, cord”). Compare Italian and Romansch corda, Romanian coardă, Spanish cuerda, French corde.

lecâ.etymology: Possibly of Germanic origin; cf. Frankish *lekkon, from Proto-Germanic *likkōną, whence Old English liccian (Modern English lick). Compare Italian leccare and French lécher.

viscôs.etymology: From Late Latin viscōsus, from Latin viscum.

velenâ.etymology: From velen; cf. also Latin venenāre. Compare Italian avvelenare.

velenôs.etymology: From Late Latin venēnōsus, from Latin venēnum. Cf. Italian velenoso.

vanzeli.etymology: From Latin evangelium, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion). Compare Italian vangelo.

fumâ.etymology: From Latin fūmāre, present active indicative of fūmō.

umid.etymology: Ultimately from Latin hūmidus, possibly via Italian umido.

fiastri.etymology: From Late Latin fīliaster, fīliastrum, from Latin fīlius.

dolorôs.etymology: From Late Latin dolōrōsus, from Latin dolor.

sanganôs.etymology: From Late Latin sanguinōsus, from Latin sanguis.

batae.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *battālia, from Latin battuālia. Compare Italian battaglia, Romanian bătaie, French bataille, Spanish batalla.

vôs.etymology: From Latin vōcem, accusative singular of vōx.

cusine.etymology: From Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna.

bolp.etymology: From Latin vulpēs, vulpem. Compare Ladin volp, Romansh vulp, Venetan bolp, volp, bolpe, Dalmatian bualp, Istriot bulpo, Italian volpe.

cusî.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin root *cusīre < *cosīre, from *cōsere, from Latin consuere. Compare Italian cucire.

cusinâ.etymology: From Late Latin cocīnāre, from Latin coquīnāre.

cuei.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cocere, from Latin coquere.

claud.etymology: From Latin clāvus, through a Vulgar Latin form *claus, with a -d- added due to influence from Latin claudō (“close”). Compare Italian chiodo, Istriot ciuodo.

ombrôs.etymology: From Latin umbrōsus; equivalent to ombre + -ôs.

ombrî.etymology: From ombre, or from a Vulgar Latin root *umbrīre, from Latin umbra. Compare Romanian umbri.

oltri.etymology: From Latin ultrā, ulter. Compare Italian oltre.

orloi.etymology: From Latin hōrologium, from Ancient Greek ὡρολόγιον (hōrológion).

cristian.etymology: Probably a learned borrowing from Latin Christiānus.

vieli.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin veclus, from Latin vetulus.

stuart.etymology: From Latin extortus. Compare Italian storto, Ladin stort.

scjadê.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *excadēre (“fall out”), from Latin ex- + cadere. Compare Italian scadere.

cjamp.etymology: From Latin campus. Compare Ladin ciamp.

cjamin.etymology: From Latin camīnus, from Ancient Greek κάμινος (káminos).

cjançon.etymology: From Latin cantiō, cantiōnem. Compare Romansh chanzun, Italian canzone, French chanson.

cjarvonâr.etymology: From cjarvon or from Latin carbōnārius.

cjastrât.etymology: From the past participle of cjastrâ, corresponding to Latin castrātus. Compare Italian castrato.

inglaçâ.etymology: From glace or from Vulgar Latin *inglaciāre, from Latin glaciāre. Compare Romanian îngheța.

dolçôr.etymology: From Late Latin dulcor, dulcōrem, from Latin dulcis.

molzi.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *mŭlgĕre, from Latin mulgēre (“milk”).

taiâ.etymology: From Late Latin tāliāre, a verb based on Latin tālea (“cutting taken from a plant”). Compare Italian tagliare.

ongule.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *ungla, from Latin ungula, from unguis.

lipare.etymology: From Latin vīpera. Compare Venetan lìpera, vìpara.

gjalinâr.etymology: From Latin gallīnārium or from gjaline.

barcje.etymology: From Late Latin barca, probably from Latin baris, from Ancient Greek βᾶρις (bâris), itself probably of Egyptian origin.

tiessidure.etymology: From tiessi. Compare Italian tessitura, Romanian țesătură, Spanish tejedura, Portuguese tecedura.

urdî.etymology: From Latin ōrdīre, collateral form of ōrdīrī.

armade.etymology: From the feminine past participle of armâ, corresponding to Medieval Latin armāta, from the feminine past participle of Latin armāre, from arma (“arms”).

vuarzine.etymology: Probably ultimately from Latin organum (“implement, instrument, tool”).

arint.etymology: From Latin argentum. Compare Italian argento, Romansh argient, Romanian argint, French argent.

zoventût.etymology: From Latin iuventūtem, juventūtem, accusative of iuventus.

agnul.etymology: From Late Latin angelus, from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos).

farinôs.etymology: From Late Latin farīnōsus, from Latin farīna.

frêt.etymology: From Latin frīgidus (“cold, cool, chilling”) (through a syncopated Vulgar Latin or Late Latin form fridus or frigdus, fricdus), from frīgeō, frīgēre (“be cold”). Compare Ladin frëit, Romansh freid, French froid, Italian freddo.

zurâ.etymology: From Latin jūrāre, iūrāre (“swear or take an oath”).

zurament.etymology: From Late Latin jūrāmentum, iūrāmentum (“oath”), from Latin iūrō. Equivalent to zurâ + -ment.

florî.etymology: From Late Latin flōrīre, from Latin flōrēre.

surîs.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *sōrīcem, *sōrīx, alteration of the Classical Latin sōrex, sōricis. Compare French souris.

genitôr.etymology: From Latin genitor, genitōrem; cf. Italian genitore.

paian.etymology: Inherited from Latin pāgānus. Compare French païen.

paiâ.etymology: From Latin pacāre. Compare Romansh pajar, French payer.

furlan.etymology: Cf. the name of the region, Friûl. Compare Italian furlano.

mangjâ.etymology: Compare Italian mangiare. Ultimately from Latin manducāre.

zuiâ.etymology: Inherited from Latin iocārī. Compare Italian giocare.

zuiadôr.etymology: From zuiâ. Compare Italian giocatore, Romansh giugadur, giujeader, Venetan xugadore, Istriot zugadur, Romanian jucător, French joueur, Portuguese jogador, Spanish and Catalan jugador.

clâf.etymology: From Latin clāvis, clāvem. Compare French clef, Romansh clav, Franco-Provençal cllâf, Dalmatian cluf.

formadi.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin fōrmāticum, from Latin fōrma (“mould”). Compare Lombard formai.

ospedâl.etymology: From Late Latin hospitālis, hospitāle (“shelter, hospice, guesthouse”), from Latin hospitālis (“hospitable”). Compare Italian ospedale, Venetan ospedal.

Pieri.etymology: From Latin Petrus, from Ancient Greek Πέτρος (Pétros).

sunâ.etymology: From Latin sonāre. Compare Romansh sunar, Italian suonare, Romanian suna, Sicilian sunari, Spanish sonar.

romôr.etymology: From Latin rūmor, rūmōrem. Compare Italian rumore.

savê.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sapēre, from Latin sapere (“taste, know”).

comprâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *comperāre, from Latin comparāre (“prepare, procure, get, purchase, obtain”).

tignî.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin tenīre, from Latin tenēre. Compare Romansh tegnair.

lôf.etymology: From Latin lupus. Compare Romansh luf, louf, Venetan lóvo, Emilian låuv, Italian lupo, Catalan llop, Spanish lobo.

vierzi.etymology: Variant of avierzi, from Latin aperīre. Cf. also Venetan vèrzar, verxar, vèrzer.

avierzi.etymology: From Latin aperīre. Compare Venetan averzir, avèrzer, avèrxer, vèrzar, Romansh avrir, Italian aperire, French ouvrir. Cf. also the related vierzi.

cuvierzi.etymology: From Latin cooperīre. Compare Venetan covèrzar, Romansh cuvrir, Italian coprire, French couvrir.

cuviert.etymology: From Latin coopertus. Compare Romansh cuvert, Italian coperto, French couvert.

jôf.etymology: From Latin jugum, iugum. Compare Venetan dóvo, Old French jof, jug, Italian giogo.

pierdi.etymology: From Latin perdere. Compare Romanian pierde, Ladin perde, Romansh perder, Italian perdere, Venetan pèrdar, Dalmatian piardro, French perdre.

nevôt.etymology: From Latin nepōs, nepōtem. Compare Venetan nevódo, neodo, Romansh nev, Italian nipote, Romanian nepot, Catalan and Occitan nebot, French neveu.

gnece.etymology: From Late Latin nepta, from Latin neptis. Compare Romansh nezza.

siôr.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *seior, contracted form of Latin senior. Compare French sieur, sire.

zinar.etymology: From Latin gener, generum, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵm̥ros, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵem-.

brût.etymology: Probably from Medieval Latin bruta (compare French bru), from Old High German brūt (“daughter-in-law, bride”), from Proto-West Germanic *brūdi (“bride, daughter-in-law”).

lagrimôs.etymology: From lagrime + -ôs or from Latin lacrimōsus.

martars.etymology: From Latin Mārtis diēs, variant of diēs Mārtis (“day of Mars”).

miercus.etymology: From Latin Mercuriī diēs, variant of diēs Mercuriī (“day of Mercury”).

joibe.etymology: From Latin Jovis diēs or Iovis diēs, variant of diēs Iovis (“Jupiter's day”).

vinars.etymology: From Latin Veneris diēs < diēs Veneris (“day of Venus”).

sabide.etymology: From Latin sabbata, from sabbatum. Compare Ladin sabeda, Romansh sonda, sanda, somda, Dalmatian sabata, Romanian sâmbătă, Italian sabato, French samedi, Spanish sábado.

domenie.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin [diēs] Dominica (literally “day of the Lord”).

straponzi.etymology: Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *extrapungere, from Latin pungere (“prick, puncture”). Cf. also Romanian străpunge.

volê.etymology: From Vulgar Latin volēre, regularized from Latin velle.

jentrade.etymology: From the feminine past participle of jentrâ. Compare Italian entrata, Ladin ntreda.

viodi.etymology: From Latin vidēre, probably through a Vulgar Latin *vidĕre.

dulî.etymology: From Latin dolēre, with a change in conjugation or possibly through a Vulgar Latin root *dolīre.

duliôs.etymology: From dulî or dulie, possibly from a Vulgar Latin *doliōsus, from Latin dolor. Compare Italian doglioso, Romanian duios.

dûs.etymology: From Latin dux, ducem, from dūcō (“to lead, guide”). Compare Italian duce, Venetan Doxe, Ligurian Dûxe. See also the doublet duche.

scuelâr.etymology: From Late Latin scholāris, from Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ).

miorâ.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin meliōrāre, a verb based on Latin melior (“better”). By surface analysis, miôr + -â.

stâ.etymology: From Latin stāre. Compare Venetan star, Ligurian stâ, Romansh star, Italian stare, Romanian sta, Dalmatian stur, Catalan and Spanish estar.

uldî.etymology: From Latin audīre. Compare Italian udire, Venetan aldir.

uldide.etymology: From the feminine past participle of uldî, corresponding to Latin audīta. Compare Romansh udida.

podê.etymology: From Vulgar Latin potēre, regularization of Latin posse.

polvar.etymology: From Latin pulverem, accusative of pulvis.

nassince.etymology: From nassi or from Latin nāscentia.

todesc.etymology: From Medieval Latin or Late Latin theodiscus, from Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz (“of the people, popular, vernacular”), from *þeudō (“people”) + *-iskaz (“-ish, -ic, -al”). Compare Italian tedesco, Venetan todesco, French thiois.

purcit.etymology: From a derivative of Latin porcus. Compare also Sardinian porchitu (“little pig, piglet”).

parêt.etymology: From Late Latin parētem, from Latin parietem m.

sclâf.etymology: From Late Latin or Medieval Latin sclavus (“slave”), from Sclavus (“Slav”), from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos), which see for more.

vincj.etymology: From Latin vīgintī, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁wih₁ḱm̥ti, from *dwi(h₁)dḱm̥ti(h₁) (“two tens, two decades”), *dwi(h₁)dḱm̥ti.

cenglâr.etymology: From an earlier *senglâr, from Vulgar Latin *singlāris, from Latin singulāris [porcus]. Compare Italian cinghiale, Occitan singlar, Catalan singlar, French sanglier.

lassâ.etymology: From Latin laxāre. Compare Italian lasciare, Romansh laschar, Neapolitan lassà, Romanian lăsa, French laisser.

jutori.etymology: From Latin adiūtōrium. Compare Romanian ajutor, Italian aiutorio.

justizie.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin jūstitia (compare Italian giustizia). Compare also justece.

justece.etymology: From just, cf. Latin iūstitia. Compare Italian giustezza, French justesse, Spanish and Portuguese justeza, Catalan and Occitan justesa, Galician and Asturian xusteza. See also justizie (“justice”).

peraule.etymology: From Late Latin, from Latin parabola (“comparison; later, speech”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ, “comparison; parable”).

nâf.etymology: From Latin nāvis, nāvem. Compare Romansh nav, French nef.

fûc.etymology: From Latin focus. Compare Romansh fiug, Venetan fógo, fóc, Dalmatian fuc, Italian fuoco, Emilian fûg, Romanian foc, Occitan fuòc, French feu, Spanish fuego.

pesâ.etymology: From Latin pēnsāre. Doublet of pensâ.

pensâ.etymology: From Latin pēnsāre (“weigh, hang”). Doublet of pensâ.

pês.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *pēsum, from Latin pēnsum.

valôr.etymology: From Latin valōrem, accusative singular of valor.

pedoli.etymology: From Late Latin peduclus < peduculus, variant of Latin pēdīculus, diminutive of pēdis.

pedoglôs.etymology: From Vulgar Latin peduclosus, from Latin peduculōsus.

civole.etymology: From Late Latin cepulla, diminutive of Latin cēpa.

neveâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *nivicāre, a verb based on Latin nivem (“snow”, noun). Compare Venetan nevegar.

neveade.etymology: From the feminine past participle of neveâ. Compare Italian nevicata.

nissun.etymology: From Latin ne ipse unum. Compare Italian nessuno, Neapolitan nisciuno, Dalmatian nenčoin, Old French neisune; compare also Romanian niciun, Spanish ninguno.

nûl.etymology: From Latin nūbilum, noun use of the neuter of the adjective nūbilus (“cloudy”), from Latin nūbēs. Compare Italian nuvolo, Romansh nivel, Venetan nùvoła, Romanian nor, Catalan núvol.

zenoli.etymology: From Late Latin genuculum, alteration of Latin geniculum, diminutive of genū (“knee”).

numar.etymology: From Latin numerus. Compare Venetan nùmaro, Romansh and Ladin numer, Italian numero, Romanian număr, French nombre.

cercli.etymology: From Latin circulus. See also circul.

pescjadôr.etymology: From pescjâ or from Latin piscātor.

pessâr.etymology: From pes, or from Latin piscārius.

buteghe.etymology: From Latin apothēca, from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē, “storehouse”).

bielece.etymology: From biel, or possibly from Vulgar Latin *bellitia, from Latin bellus. Compare Italian bellezza, Romansh baleztgia, Occitan belesa, Catalan bellesa, Spanish belleza, Portuguese beleza, Sicilian biddizza, Sardinian bellesa.

glosses_en: to return, go back, come back

bevidôr.etymology: From bevi, or from Latin bibitor, bibitōrem.

bevût.etymology: Past participle of bevi. Compare Italian bevuto.

bevude.etymology: From the feminine past participle of bevi. Compare Italian bevuta.

cirî.etymology: From Latin quaerere, with a change in conjugation or possibly through a Vulgar Latin root *quaerīre. Compare French quérir, Sardinian chèrri, Walloon cweri, Italian chiedere, Romanian cere, Spanish querer.

cercjâ.etymology: From Late Latin circāre, from Latin circa, circus. Cognate with Ladin ciarcë.

crodince.etymology: From crodi, or possibly from Late Latin crēdentia, from Latin crēdens. Compare also the possible doublet credince.

credince.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin crēdentia, from Latin crēdens. Compare Italian credenza. Possibly a doublet of crodince.

glosses_en: to inflate, blow up, puff up, swell

umbriçon.etymology: From a derivative of Latin umbilīcus.

meracul.etymology: Ultimately from Latin mīrāculum. Compare Italian miracolo.

zâl.etymology: Ultimately from Latin galbinus, possibly through Italian giallo, itself from Old French jalne. Compare also Venetan xało, zało, Istriot zalo.

cinise.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *cinisia, from Latin cinis.

veture.etymology: Ultimately from Latin vectūra. Compare Italian vettura, French voiture.

capî.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *capīre, from Latin capere (“to take in, understand”). Compare Italian capire, Ladin capir, Romansh chapir, Venetan capir.

zontâ.etymology: From a derivative of Latin iūnctus, perhaps through Vulgar Latin *iūnctāre (a root). Compare zonte. Compare Italian giuntare, Venetan xontar, Spanish juntar, Portuguese juntar.

zonte.etymology: From Latin iūncta < iūnctus. Compare Ladin jonta, Venetan xonta, Italian giunta, Spanish and Portuguese junta.

zontadure.etymology: From the feminine past participle of zontâ.

scuedi.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *excotere, from Latin excutere. Compare Italian scuotere, Romanian scoate, Dalmatian scutro.

pustot.etymology: From Slovene pustota (compare Old Church Slavonic поустота (pustota, “emptiness, void”)).

tosc.etymology: From Latin tuscus (“Etruscan”), in the context of Vicus Tuscus in Rome, whose inhabitants had a bad reputation. Compare Venetan tosco (“boor”), Spanish tosco (“crude, rough, uncouth”), Catalan tosc (“rough, coarse”), compare also Albanian t

menâ.etymology: From Latin mināre, collateral form of minārī.

preâ.etymology: From Latin precor. Compare Italian pregare, French prier, Venetan pregar, Catalan pregar, Occitan prejar, Sicilian prijari.

gîr.etymology: From Latin gȳrus, from Ancient Greek γῦρος (gûros).

plovi.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *plovere, from Classical Latin pluere.

taront.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *torundus, from Latin rotundus.

piruç.etymology: From a diminutive of Latin pirum.

altece.etymology: From alt. Compare Italian altezza, Venetan altézsa.

alçâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *altiāre, derived from Latin altus (“high”).

fuarpis.etymology: From Latin forficem, accusative of forfex.

roseâ.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rōsicāre, frequentative based on Latin rōdere. Compare Venetan roxegar, Italian rosicare.

roseadôr.etymology: From roseâ. Compare Catalan rosegador, Italian roditore, French rongeur.

tindi.etymology: From Latin tendere (“to stretch, stretch out, distend, extend”). Compare Italian tendere, Romanian tinde, French tendre.

scjaldâ.etymology: From Late Latin excaldāre, from Latin cal(i)dus (“hot”).

glosses_en: to seem, to look, to appear

benvignût.etymology:
ben + vignût, past participle of vignî.
Compare Italian benvenuto, Venetan benvegnuo, Romansh bainvegni, French bienvenue, Catalan benvingut, Occitan benvengut, Piedmontese bin-ëvnù, Sicilian binvinutu.

cjadree.etymology: From Latin cathēdra (possibly through a Vulgar Latin variant cathégra, attested in Pompeiian inscriptions), ultimately from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra). Compare Romansh chadregia, Lombard and Piedmontese cadrega, Ligurian and Venetan c

insumiâsi.etymology: From in + sium or from Latin somniāre.

distruzi.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *destrugere, from Classical Latin dēstruō, from dē- (“un-, de-”) + struō (“to build”).

narile.etymology: Ultimately from Latin nāris. Compare Italian narice, French narine.

lezion.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin lēctiō, lēctiōnem.

starnudâ.etymology: From Latin sternūtāre, frequentative of sternuō. Compare Venetan starnudar, Italian starnutare, Romansh starnüdar, Romanian strănuta, Catalan esternudar, French éternuer.

batiâ.etymology: From Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptīzāre, from Ancient Greek βαπτῑ́ζω (baptī́zō).

glosses_en: to flee, run away, escape, make off
fuî.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *fugīre, from Latin fugere.

glosses_en: to escape, run away, flee, get away, fly off
scjampâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *excampāre, variant of *excappāre, a verb based on Late Latin cappa (“cloak”).

scurtâ.etymology: From Late Latin excurtāre, from Latin curtāre.

glosses_en: to pass (i.e. the time), spend, go by
to pass, pass through, get through
passâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *passāre, derived from Latin passus (“step”, noun).

pae.etymology: From Latin palea. Compare Venetan paja, Italian paglia, Istriot paja, Romanian paie, French paille, Catalan palla, Spanish paja.

ufrî.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *offerīre, from Latin offerre.

ufierte.etymology: From the feminine of the past participle of ufrî, or from Medieval Latin, Late Latin offerta, ultimately from Latin offerō. Compare Romansh and Italian offerta, Portuguese and Spanish oferta, Catalan oferta, Sicilian ufferta, Sardinian ofer

glosses_en: to dine, have dinner, have supper

feride.etymology: From the feminine past participle of ferî. Compare Italian ferita, Romansh frida, Portuguese ferida, Spanish herida.

fêl.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *felem m or f, from Latin fel n.

salâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin root *salāre, from a change in conjugation of Latin salīre (“to salt”), from sal. Compare Italian salare, French saler, Romanian săra, Spanish, Portuguese, and Catalan salar, Sicilian salari.

zucar.etymology: From Arabic سُكَّر (sukkar) (probably borrowed via one or multiple Italo-Romance languages), from Persian شکر (šakar), from Middle Persian škl (/⁠šakar⁠/), from Sanskrit शर्करा (śarkarā). Compare Venetan sùcaro, Istriot soûcaro, Italian zuc

pôre.etymology: From Latin pavor, pavōrem. Compare Italian paura, French peur.

maçâ.etymology: Compare Romansh mazzar, Venetan masar, Italian ammazzare, Istriot masà, Occitan massar, compare also Spanish mazar.

rispuindi.etymology: From Late Latin respondere, from Latin respondēre. Compare Ladin respuender, Romansh respuonder.

mandule.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *amandula, from Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē).

cjosse.etymology: From Latin causa. Doublet of cause.

glosses_en: to be obliged, compelled, or forced to; must, have to
dovê.etymology: From Latin dēbēre (“owe”). Compare Ladin dovei, Venetan dover, Italian dovere, French devoir, Dalmatian dovar.

uciel.etymology: From Late Latin aucellus m (“little bird”), a diminutive ultimately based on Latin avis f (“bird”). Compare Romansh utschè, Venetan oxeło.

cierf.etymology: From Latin cervus. Compare Ladin cerf, Romansh tschierv, French cerf, Venetan and Italian cervo.

cence.etymology: Probably from a conflation of Latin absentia and sine. Compare Italian senza, French sans.

fasûl.etymology: From Latin phaseolus, ultimately from Ancient Greek φάσηλος (phásēlos).

salvâ.etymology: From Late Latin salvō, salvāre (“I save”), from Latin salvus.

glesie.etymology: From Latin ecclēsia, from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía).

daspò.etymology: From Latin de post. Compare Istriot duopo, Venetan dapò, Dalmatian dapú, Italian dopo, Romanian după, French depuis, Spanish después, Portuguese depois.

antîc.etymology: From Latin antīquus, perhaps (considering the /-k/) via Italian amico. Compare Friulian amì < Latin amīcus.

paîs.etymology: From Late Latin pāgēnsis (“inhabitant of a district”), from Latin pāgus (“village; district”). Compare Romansh pajais, Venetan pajès, Istriot pais, Italian paese, Catalan país, French pays, Portuguese país, Spanish país, Sicilian paisi.

vuardâ.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin wardāre.

comedon.etymology: Ultimately from Latin cubitum, probably from a derivative form or with an additional suffix in Friulian. Cf. Italian gomito, Istriot cumio, Venetan comio, gòmio.

menaçâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *mināciāre (“threaten”), from minācia (“threat”), from Latin mināx, mināciae. Compare Italian minacciare, French menacer.

lâc.etymology: From Latin lacus, from Proto-Indo-European *lókus (“lake, pool”).

incuin.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *incudinem, from Latin incus, incudem.

aiar.etymology: From Latin aēr. Compare Romansh ajer, Venetan aiere, Italian aria, Romanian aer, French air.

martiel.etymology: From Late Latin martellus, from Latin marculus, diminutive of marcus, or from malleus.

condusi.etymology: From Latin condūcere (“lead, bring or draw together”).

gjoldi.etymology: Inherited from Latin gaudēre. Compare Romansh giudair.

bisugne.etymology:
