Frankish *bisunnijabor.
Vulgar Latin *bisonium
Friulian bisugne
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bisonium, borrowed from Frankish *bisunnija.

açâr.etymology: From Late Latin aciārium, from Latin aciēs. Compare Venetan açal, Romansh atschal, Italian acciaio, Catalan acer, French acier, Galician aceiro, Occitan acièr, Portuguese aço, Sicilian azzaru, Spanish acero.

açâl.etymology: From Late Latin aciāle, Late Latin aciārium, from Latin aciēs. Compare Venetan açal, asal, azhal, Romansh atschal, itschal.

debul.etymology: From Latin dēbilis. Compare Italian debole.

façolet.etymology: Diminutive derived from Vulgar Latin *faciolum, from Latin facies (“face”). Compare Romansh fazielet, fazalet, Venetan fasołeto, Italian fazzoletto, Istriot fassulito, Sicilian fazzulettu.

glosses_en: to shake, shake up, beat, knock, bang
sbati.etymology: From bati, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *exbattere, from Latin battuere. Compare Italian sbattere, Venetan sbàter, sbàtar, Sicilian sbàttiri, cf. also Romanian zbate.

glosses_en: to close, close off; to end, wind up
sierâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *serrāre, from Late Latin serāre (“fasten, bolt”), from Latin sera (“bolt, crossbar”).

ovâ.etymology: From ûf or from a Vulgar Latin root *ōvāre, from Latin ōvum. Compare Romanian oua, Spanish ovar.

clucî.etymology: Possibly ultimately from Latin glocīre (“to cluck”); compare also Romanian cloci, Bulgarian kloči.

nancje.etymology: ni + ancje. Compare Italian neanche, Venetan gnanca, nianca, nanca, Istriot gnanca.

ocje.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *avica, from Classical Latin avis (“bird”). Compare Romansh oca, ocha, auca, Venetan and Italian oca, Dalmatian jauca, Istriot uoca, Occitan auca, Catalan oca, French oie.

poleç.etymology: From a diminutive of Latin pullus.

fieste.etymology: From Late Latin fēsta, from Latin fēsta, plural of fēstum.

lizêr.etymology: Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *leviārius, from Latin levis; compare French léger, Italian leggero, Ladin lesier, Puter and Vallader Romansh liger, Venetan lixiero, Sicilian liggeru.

cussì.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *eccum sīc. Compare Dalmatian coisa, Italian così, Istriot cussèi, Venetan cusì.

cjampanîli.etymology: From cjampane. Compare Italian campanile, Venetan canpaniłe, Istriot canpaneîl, Spanish campanil.

cjamese.etymology: From Late Latin camisia, from Transalpine Gaulish, of Germanic origin, from Proto-Germanic *hamiþiją.

insegnâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin insignāre, from Latin signō.

cjapiel.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin cappellus, diminutive from Late Latin cappa. Compare Romansh chapè.

nassût.etymology: Past participle of nassi. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *nāscūtus, from Latin nāscor. Compare Romansh naschiu, Ladin nascù, Piedmontese nassù, Dalmatian nascoit, Romanian născut, Catalan and Occitan nascut.

sangloçâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *singlutiāre, from singultiāre, from Latin singultāre, from singultus. The (Vulgar) Latin was altered under the influence of gluttiō, gluttīre (“to swallow”). Compare Italian singhiozzare, Romansh sanglotter, French sanglo

sangloç.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *singlutius, ultimately from Latin singultus, influenced by gluttiō. Compare Italian singhiozzo, Romansh sanglut, Venetan sangiuto, French sanglot.

cjanaipe.etymology: From Vulgar Latin, Late Latin canapa, from Latin cannabis, from Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis).

cjavrûl.etymology: From Latin capreolus. Compare French chevreuil, Italian capriolo.

sponzi.etymology: From Latin expungere. Compare Ladin sponjer.

cjavron.etymology: Augmentative of cjavre. Compare Venetan cavron, Italian caprone, French chevron, Spanish cabrón.

cjavece.etymology: From Vulgar Latin capitia, from the neuter plural of capitium (reanalyzed as a feminine singular). Compare Venetan caveça, Italian cavezza.

leç.etymology: From Latin lēgem, accusative of lēx.

lengaç.etymology: Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *linguāticum, from Latin lingua. Judging by the ending, borrowed through either Occitan (possibly via Italian) or French.

cjariâ.etymology: From Late Latin carricāre, from Latin carrus.

cjarie.etymology: From cjariâ. Compare Italian carica, Romansh chargia, tgargia, Ladin cèria, Venetan carga, French charge.

otante.etymology: From Latin octāgintā, variant of octōgintā.

cjarte.etymology: From Latin charta, from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, “papyrus, paper”).

netâ.etymology: A verb based on net (“clean”), or inherited directly from Latin Latin nitidō. Compare Italian nettare, Venetan netar.

pietin.etymology: From Latin pecten, pectinem. Compare Italian pettine, Romanian pieptene, French peigne.

grivi.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin grevem, alteration of Latin gravem.

neâ.etymology: From Latin negāre. Compare Italian negare, French nier.

etât.etymology: From Latin aetās, aetātem. Compare Italian etade. Doublet of ete.

zunâ.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin derivative of Late Latin ieiūnāre, from Latin ieiūnus. Compare Old Italian giunare.

dizun.etymology: From Vulgar Latin, from Latin jejunium, from ieiunium, with the shift in Latin je- or ie- to de-, and later di- in Friulian. Compare Italian digiuno, Catalan dejuni.

spietâ.etymology: From Latin spectāre, or from aspectō, aspectāre. Compare Italian aspettare, Romansh spetgar, Venetan spetar, aspetar.

bagnâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *baneare, from Late Latin balneāre, from Latin balneum. Compare Italian bagnare, Venetan bagnar, Catalan banyar, French baigner.

cjastine.etymology: From Latin castanea, from Ancient Greek καστάνεια (kastáneia).

cjastinâr.etymology: From cjastine. Compare French châtaignier. Cf. also Medieval Latin castanearius.

cjastiâ.etymology: From Latin castīgāre (“to chastise, reprimand”). Compare Romansh chastiar, French châtier.

infassâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *infasciāre or from in + fassâ, from Late Latin fasciō, fasciāre, ultimately from Latin fascia. Compare Venetan infasar, Istriot infasà, Romanian înfășa, Italian fasciare.

fassâ.etymology: From Late Latin fasciāre, from Latin fascia.

rivâ.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin adrīpāre.

scuvierzi.etymology: From s- + cuvierzi. Compare Italian scoprire.

miedi.etymology: From Latin medicus. The -ie- may be an unexpected outcome (cf. pît < Latin pĕdem); if so, there may have been influence from Venetan m(i)edego.

concuistâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *conquisitāre, from Latin conquisitus, past participle of conquīrō. Compare Italian conquistare, Catalan and Spanish conquistar.

cjalderie.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin caldāria (“cooking-pot”), derived from Latin caldus (“hot”).

fioç.etymology: From fi (“son”). Compare Italian figlioccio, Venetan fioso, fioço.

dûl.etymology: Probably from Late Latin dolus, a derivative of Latin dolor. Cf. also Vulgar Latin *dolium from cordolium. Compare Italian duolo, French deuil, Spanish duelo.

balâ.etymology: From Late Latin ballō, borrowed from, or related to, Ancient Greek βαλλίζω (ballízō), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH- (“to throw”).

bajâ.etymology: Possibly ultimately from Latin baubari, or of imitative origin. Compare Italian abbaiare, Venetan bajar, bagiar, Dalmatian bajur, French aboyer.

slançâ.etymology: From s- (< Latin ex-) + Late Latin lanceāre, from Latin lancea. Compare Italian slanciare, lanciare, French élancer, lancer, Venetan slansar, lansar.

leâl.etymology: From Latin lēgālis. Doublet of legâl.

legâl.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin lēgālis. Doublet of leâl.

lealtât.etymology: From leâl. Compare Italian lealtà, Catalan lleialtat, French loyauté, Spanish lealtad.

lessâ.etymology: From Late Latin elixō, elixāre, from Latin lixa (“hot water”), cf. elixus. Compare Italian lessare, Venetan lesar, Spanish elijar.

stagn.etymology: From Latin stannum, stagnum, of Celtic origin.

glosses_en: a male given name, equivalent to English Alexander
Lissandri.etymology: From Latin Alexander, from Ancient Greek Ἀλέξανδρος (Aléxandros).

capitâl.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin capitālis. Doublet of cjavedâl (“andiron”).

cjariesâr.etymology: From cjariese. Compare French cerisier, Catalan cirerer, Portuguese cerejeira.

cjariese.etymology: From Vulgar Latin ceresia, from the neuter plural of Late Latin ceresium, from Latin cerasium, from Ancient Greek κεράσιον (kerásion, “cherry”), from κερασός (kerasós, “bird cherry”), ultimately possibly of Anatolian origin.

domandâ.etymology: From Latin demandāre. Compare Italian domandare, Ladin domanèr, Romansh dumandar, Venetan domandar.

messedâ.etymology: Probably from a Vulgar Latin *miscitāre, from Latin misceō (“to mix”). Compare Ladin mescedèr, Venetan mesedar, Romansh mischedar, maschadar, archaic or literary Italian miscidare, mescidare; cf. also mestare.

tocjâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *toccāre, *tuccāre (“strike, touch”), of Germanic or onomatopoetic origin.

tastâ.etymology: Possibly from Vulgar Latin *tastō, *tastāre, from taxitō, frequentative of Late Latin taxō, from Classical Latin tangō (“to touch”). Compare Venetan tastar, Italian tastare, Catalan and Occitan tastar, Old French taster, Sicilian tastari.

tarlîs.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *trilicius, from Latin trilix.

vistî.etymology: From Latin vestīre, present active indicative of vestiō.

glosses_en: Genoa (a port city and comune, the capital of the Metropolitan City of Genoa and the region of Liguria, Italy)
Genoa (a metropolitan city of Liguria, established in 2015; in full, the Metropolitan City of Genoa)

calcagn.etymology: From Latin calcāneum, possibly a borrowing or semi-learned term, or alternatively through the intermediate of Italian calcagno.

caglâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *coaglāre, *quaglāre, from Latin coāgulāre.

çore.etymology: Uncertain. Compare Sicilian ciaula, Neapolitan ciàula, Tarantino ciola, cf. also Romanian cioară, Albanian sorrë, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Albanian *tšārnā.

çavate.etymology: Ultimately of Turkish origin. Compare Italian ciabatta.

çucje.etymology: From Late Latin cucutia, through metathesis and apheresis (or possibly through the Italian equivalent, zucca), from Latin cucurbita. Compare Romansh zücha, zetga, Italian zucca, cocuzza, Venetan suca, zuca, zhuca.

cavalîr.etymology: Borrowed from Italian cavaliere, French cavalier, or Old Occitan [Term?].

glosses_en: groom (one who cares for horses), hostler
cjavalâr.etymology: From cjaval, or possibly Late Latin caballārius, from Latin caballus.

cjavalgjâ.etymology: From Late Latin caballicāre, from Latin caballus.

faiâr.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *fāgārius, a derivative of Latin fagus. Cognate with Venetan faghèr, faghèra, fagaro, Dalmatian faguor.

sponze.etymology: From Latin spongia, from Ancient Greek σπογγιά (spongiá).

persembul.etymology: From Latin petroselinum, from Ancient Greek πετροσέλινον (petrosélinon), from πέτρα (pétra, “stone”) + σέλινον (sélinon, “celery”).

tampieste.etymology: From Latin tempesta, tempestās. Compare Venetan tenpesta, tompesta (“hail, hailstorm”), Romansh tempesta, tempiasta (“hailstorm”).

insium.etymology: Cf. sium, insumiâsi. Compare also Venetan insonio (“dream”), insogno.

sparc.etymology: From Latin asparagus, from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος (aspáragos).

glosses_en: Slovenia (a country on the Balkan Peninsula in Central Europe)

batisim.etymology: From Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin baptismus, baptismum, from Ancient Greek βαπτισμός (baptismós).

vuê.etymology: From Latin hodiē. Compare Dalmatian vai.

saût.etymology: From Latin sabūcus, variant of sambūcus.

muscli.etymology: From Latin mūscus, probably through a diminutive Vulgar Latin root *mūsclus, from syncopation of an earlier *mūsculus. Compare Italian muschio, Romanian mușchi.

basavon.etymology: Cf. von. Compare Italian bisavo, bisavolo.

muardi.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *mordĕre, from Latin mordēre.

smorseâ.etymology: From s- (< Latin ex-) + Latin morsicāre.

imprestâ.etymology: From Latin praestāre, with a prefix added later. Compare Italian imprestare, Venetan inprestar.

svindicâ.etymology: From s- (from Latin ex-) + Latin vindicāre.

glosses_en: to remove or take off shoes
discolçâ.etymology: Probably from Late Latin discalceāre, from Latin calceō. Perhaps influenced by Latin disculciāre; cf. discolç. Compare Romanian desculța, variant of descălța, Sardinian iscultzare, iscurtare, iscrutzai.

discolç.etymology: From discolçâ, or from a Vulgar Latin root *disculceus or *discalceus, itself from Late Latin discalceō (or from Latin dis- + calceus), or less likely from disculciātus, but possibly influenced by it. Compare Venetan descolz, Dalmatian disc

cjalce.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin calcea, from Latin calceus (“shoe”).

glosses_en: to put on or wear shoes

culine.etymology: From Late Latin collīna, from the feminine of Latin collīnus, from collis (“hill”) + -ina, from Proto-Indo-European *kl̥Hnís (“top, hill, rock”).

gjambe.etymology: From Late Latin gamba (“hoof”). Compare Italian gamba, Romansh tgomba, chomma, French jambe, Venetan ganba.

cjavile.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *cāvicla < *cāvicula, from Latin clavicula. Compare Italian cavicchia, Occitan cavilha, French cheville. See also the doublets cavicje (borrowed from Italian) and clavìcule (borrowed from Latin).

smeralt.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *smaraldus, *smaraudus, alteration of Latin smaragdus, from Ancient Greek σμάραγδος (smáragdos).

rèdine.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin retina, ultimately from Latin retineō (“hold back”).

boâr.etymology: From Vulgar Latin, Late Latin bovārius or boārius (“cow herder”), from Latin bovārius, boārius (“of cattle”), from bōs.

piorâr.etymology: piore + -âr, or possibly corresponding to Latin pecorārius.

lotadôr.etymology: lotâ + -dôr, or from Latin luctator, luctatōrem.

glosses_en: to drive out, kick out, expel, chase out
cjaçâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *captiāre, from Latin captus. Compare Italian cacciare.

trimâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *tremāre, from Classical Latin tremere.

trimulâ.etymology: From Late Latin tremulāre (“shake, tremble”), ultimately from Latin tremere.

glosses_en: to dry, to wipe, to mop

ricete.etymology: From Latin recepta, feminine of receptus (“received”), from perfect passive participle of recipiō (“to receive”).

sentâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *sedentāre, from Latin sedens, present participle of sedeō.

pendâ.etymology: Ultimately from Latin pendeō, pendēre, with a change in conjugation. Compare Venetan pendar, Italian pendere.

cjapâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *clapāre, from metathesis of *caplāre, contracted form of Late Latin capulāre, from Latin capulum. Compare Italian chiappare, Venetan ciapar, Lombard ciapà, Ladin giapé, Romansh tgapar.

bussade.etymology: From the feminine past participle of bussâ.

gambiâ.etymology: From Late Latin cambiāre, from Latin cambīre.

sgambiâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *excambiāre, from Latin ex- + Late Latin cambiāre. Cf. Italian scambiare.

corvat.etymology: From a derivative of Latin corvus.

glosses_en: to press; to press down on; stomp

batecul.etymology: Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *battuāculum, but borrowed through some intermediate source (the /k/ would be unexpected otherwise). Compare Venetan batòcolo. Doublet of batel.

batocj.etymology: Probably borrowed from Venetan batocio, batoc, from Vulgar Latin *bat(t)uāculum. Cf. Italian batacchio.

sbadaiâ.etymology: From s- + Vulgar Latin *bataculō, a derivative of batō (“to yawn”). Compare Venetan sbadagiar, Italian sbadigliare.

cuargnâl.etymology: Ultimately from Latin cornus, possibly through a diminutive form corneulus; compare Italian corniolo, Venetan crognoło.

cuargnolâr.etymology: Related to cuargnâl, cuargnul. Ultimately from Latin cornus. Compare Venetan cornołaro, French cornouiller, Catalan corneller.

cuargnul.etymology: Ultimately from Latin cornus. Related to cuargnâl, cuargnolâr.

sanzit.etymology: From a derivative of Latin sanguis (“blood”). Compare Italian sanguinella, sanguine, Catalan sanguinyol, Portuguese sanguinho, Romanian sânger.

crevâ.etymology: From Latin crepāre. Compare the doublet crepâ.

crepâ.etymology: Probably from Italian crepare, ultimately from Latin crepō. Cognates include Romanian crăpa and French crever. Compare the doublet crevâ.

crevadure.etymology: From crevâ, or from Late Latin crepātūra, from Latin crepō.

codogn.etymology: From Latin cotōneum, from Ancient Greek κυδώνιον (kudṓnion).

vacjâr.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin vaccārius.

comandâ.etymology: From Latin commandāre, variant of commendāre.

cristianitât.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin Christiānitās, Christiānitātem, from Latin Christiānus (“Christian”).

cristianisim.etymology: From Late Latin Christianismus, from Christus.

glosses_en: Attaches to an adjective to form the corresponding abstract noun.

cesel.etymology: From Old French cisel. Compare Italian cesello.

bontât.etymology: From Latin bonitās, bonitātem, corresponding to bon + -tât.

crudeltât.etymology: From Latin crūdēlitās, crūdēlitātem. Corresponds to crudêl + -tât.

cjâtif.etymology: From Latin captīvus. Compare Italian cattivo, Venetan cativo, French chétif.

glosses_en: to place, sit, put, position, arrange

falcuç.etymology: From a diminutive of Late Latin falcō (cf. the suffix -uç from -uceus).

primevere.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin prīma vēra (“early spring”), from Latin prīmus (“first”) + vēr (“spring”). Compare Italian primavera, Romansh primavaira.

sierade.etymology: From the feminine past participle of sierâ (“to close, shut, end”).

discjariâ.etymology: From Late Latin discarricāre, from carricāre, from Latin carrus.

sierât.etymology: Past participle of sierâ, cf. Latin serātus.

ducât.etymology: From Medieval Latin ducātus, from Latin dux.

sorecee.etymology: From Latin supercilia, plural of supercilium.

disleâ.etymology: From dis- + leâ, or from Vulgar Latin disligāre, from Latin dis- + ligō (“tie, bind”). Compare Ladin deslier, Venetan desligar, Italian slegare, French délier, Spanish desligar, desliar, Catalan deslligar, Romanian dezlega.

someâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *similiāre, a verb derived from Latin similis (“similar”).

someant.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *similiantem, present participle of *similiāre, a verb based on Latin similis (“similar”). By surface analysis, someâ + -ant.

someance.etymology: someâ + -ance. Compare Venetan somejansa, Italian somiglianza, Catalan and Occitan semblança, French ressemblance (Old French semblance) Spanish semejanza, Portuguese semelhança.

scovâ.etymology: From Late Latin scōpō, scōpāre (“I brush or sweep away”), from Latin scōpae (“broom”).

glosses_en: To do something wrong or badly
malfâ.etymology: mal + fâ, or from Latin malefacere.

malfat.etymology: Past participle of malfâ, corresponding to mal + fat, or from Latin malefactus.

malfatôr.etymology: From Late Latin malefactor, malefactōrem, from Latin maleficiō.

benfatôr.etymology: From Late Latin benefactor, benefactōrem, from Latin benefaciō.

convidâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *convitāre, present active infinitive of *convitō, from Latin invītō (“to invite”).

zimul.etymology: From Latin gemellus, diminutive of geminus.

zenevre.etymology: From Vulgar Latin ziniperus, from Latin iūniperus.

sielzi.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *exēligere, from Latin ex (“out of, from”) + ēligere.

sielt.etymology: Past participle of sielzi, corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *exeltus < *exelctus < *exēlēctus, from Latin ex (“out of, from”) + ēlēctus (“picked, chosen, elected”). Compare Italian scelto, Venetan sièlto; cf. also French élit.

glendon.etymology: Probably from Vulgar Latin *lēndis, lēndinem or *lēndō, from Latin lēns, lēndem (“nit”). Compare Venetan léndena, géndena.

gnovitât.etymology: From Latin novitās, novitātem, equivalent to gnûf + -itât.

noglâr.etymology: From a derivative of Latin nux. Compare Venetan noxełar, noxełer, nisołar.

Pasche.etymology: From Latin Pascha, from Ancient Greek πάσχα (páskha).

glosses_en: to sharpen up, make wiser or more expert
discjantâ.etymology: dis- + cjantâ; possibly corresponds to a Vulgar Latin discantāre, from Latin dis- + cantō. Compare Venetan descantar, Romanian descânta; cf. also French déchanter.

soflet.etymology: From soflâ. Compare Italian soffietto, Venetan supieto, French soufflet.

stiç.etymology: Ultimately from Latin tītiō, with a prefix added. Compare Italian stizza, from stizzo, older variant of tizzo, Venetan stizh, stisón.

bugnigul.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin derivative of Latin umbīlicus, probably *umbilīculus. Compare Venetan bonigolo, bunigolo, Occitan embonilh, embonígol, Catalan llombrígol.

vedran.etymology: Probably inherited from Latin veterānus, probably through the syncopated Vulgar Latin or Late Latin form vetrānus. Compare Old Venetan vetrano, Vegliot Dalmatian vetrun, Aromanian bătrân (“old, aged”).

granç.etymology: Ultimately from Latin cancer, cancrum, possibly through a diminutive Vulgar Latin form cancrulus, *cranc(u)lus. Compare Italian granchio, Venetan granso.

polpôs.etymology: From Late Latin pulpōsus, from Latin pulpa. Equivalent to polpe + -ôs.

masanâ.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin māchināre (“mill, grind”), a verb based on Latin māchina (“device, mill”), an early borrowing from Ancient Greek. Compare Venetan masnar~maxenar, Dalmatian macnur, Italian macinare. Morphological doublet of machinâ

ploiôs.etymology: ploie + -ôs, or from Latin pluviōsus. Compare Italian piovoso, Romanian ploios, Catalan plujós, French pluvieux.

fersorie.etymology: From Late Latin frixōria (“frying-pan”), from Latin frigere (“fry”).

tecje.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *tegla, from Latin tēgula, possibly through Venetan técia; compare also Italian teglia, Dalmatian tacla.

cjatâ.etymology: From Latin captāre. Compare Romansh chattar, cattar, Venetan catar.

pernîs.etymology: From Latin perdīx (“partridge”), from Ancient Greek πέρδιξ (pérdix, “partridge”).

stagjon.etymology: Ultimately from Latin stātiō, stātiōnem, possibly through the intermediate of Italian stagione.

pitôr.etymology: Ultimately from Latin pictor, pictōrem. Cf. Italian pittore.

gomitâ.etymology: From Latin vomitāre, frequentative of vomō (“spew”). Compare Venetan gomitar, Dalmatian gomituor, dialectal Portuguese gomitar.

savalon.etymology: From Latin sabulō, sabulōnem. Compare Romansh sablun, Dalmatian sablaun.

rindi.etymology: From Late Latin rendere, from Latin reddere. Compare Romansh render.

intosseâ.etymology: From Late Latin or Medieval Latin intoxicāre, from Latin toxicō, from toxicus. Compare Venetan intosegar, Italian intossicare.

fogolâr.etymology: From Late Latin foculāris, from Latin focus. Compare Venetan fogołaro, Italian focolare.

cjiscjel.etymology: From Latin castellum, diminutive of castrum.

signôr.etymology: Ultimately from Latin senior, seniōrem. Compare Italian signore. Cf. also siôr.

famei.etymology: Derivative of famee (“family”). Compare Venetan famegio, Italian famiglio.

jerbôs.etymology: From jerbe + -ôs, or from Latin herbōsus.

riul.etymology: From Latin rīvulus. Compare Italian rivolo.

lanôs.etymology: lane + -ôs, or possibly from Latin lānōsus.

budiel.etymology: From Latin botellus, diminutive of botulus.

tosâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *tonsāre, frequentative of Latin tondeō, through its past participle, tonsus. Compare Italian tosare.

cjantadôr.etymology: cjantâ + -dôr, or from Latin cantator, cantatōrem.

glosses_en: To run or operate (a business etc)

animâl.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin animal, animālis. Compare the inherited doublet nemâl.

vogâ.etymology: Probably from Latin vocāre, or alternatively of Germanic origin. Compare Italian vogare, Venetan vogar, French voguer.

remâ.etymology: From rem. Compare Venetan remar, Italian remare.

vualîf.etymology: Probably from a Vulgar Latin *aequalīvus, from Latin aequālis. Compare Romansh guliv, gualiv, Venetan guałivo.

olsâ.etymology: From Late Latin ausāre, frequentative from Latin audēre. Compare Venetan olsar.

lissie.etymology: From Latin lixīva, noun use of the adjective lixīvus (“made into lye”), from the use aqua lixīva. Compare Italian lisciva, Sicilian liscìa, Romanian leșie, French lessive, Spanish lejía.

plantagn.etymology: From Latin plantāgō, plantāginem. Compare Italian piantaggine, French plantain.

marmul.etymology: From Latin marmor (with dissimilation), from Ancient Greek μάρμαρος (mármaros, “marble”).

scudiele.etymology: From Latin scutella, diminutive of scutra.

pôl.etymology: From Latin pōpulus, through a Vulgar Latin derivative form.

stravieli.etymology: stra- + vieli. Compare Italian stravecchio, Romanian străvechi.

temporâl.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin temporālis. Compare Italian temporale.

stravuelzi.etymology: From stra- + Latin volvō. Cf. Italian stravolgere.

trute.etymology: From Late Latin tructa, possibly from Ancient Greek τρώκτης (trṓktēs).

seselâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *sicilāre, from Latin sicilis. Compare Dalmatian seclur.

jemplâ.etymology: Ultimately from Latin implēre, with a change in verb class. In light of its Romance neighbours reflecting Vulgar Latin *implīre, the Friulian form may have passed through such a stage as well.

cerfoi.etymology: Cf. Latin trifolium, calque of Ancient Greek τρίφυλλον (tríphullon); see also caprifolium. Compare Italian trifoglio, Venetan strafòjo.

glosses_en: quantity of small things, or things of little value, trifles, scraps, bits, etc.
minuçae.etymology: Related to minût, sminuçâ. Possibly from Vulgar Latin *minūtiālia, from Latin minūtia. Compare Italian minuzzaglia, Old French menuisaille, Aromanian minutsalji, Portuguese miuçalha.

Dionis.etymology: From Latin Dionysus (“Dionysus”), from Ancient Greek Διόνυσος (Diónusos).

glosses_en: to harvest or gather grapes for winemaking

avualitât.etymology: avuâl + -itât, or from Latin aequālitās, aequālitātem.

dedâl.etymology: From Late Latin digitāle, from Latin digitālis (“digital”).

pelâ.etymology: From Latin pilāre (“to deprive of hair”).

glosses_en: to remove hair or fur from
spelâ.etymology: From - + pêl, or related to pelâ. Compare Italian spelare.

dodis.etymology: From Latin duodecim. Compare Ladin dodesc, Romansh dudesch.

tredis.etymology: From Latin trēdecim. Compare Ladin tredesc, Romansh tredesch.

soridi.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *subrīdĕre, from Latin subrīdēre.

nulôr.etymology: Probably from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin olor, olōrem, itself from Latin odor, influenced by oleō. The initial n- likely became attached due to the indefinite article un (“a, an”) often preceding it. Compare Spanish, Catalan, and Occitan olor

odôr.etymology: From Latin odor, odōrem, possibly taken as a semi-learned term. Compare Italian odore, Venetan odor. Cf. also Friulian nulôr.

reâl.etymology: Ultimately from Latin rēgālem, perhaps via Italian reale, which was borrowed from Old French reial. Doublet of regâl, which was also borrowed.

leament.etymology: leâ + -ment, or possibly from Latin ligāmentum.

cusidure.etymology: cusî + -dure. Compare Italian cucitura, Venetan cuxidura.

agadôs.etymology: Related to aghe. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *aquatōsus, from Latin aquatus (“diluted, watered down, watery”), from aquor (“get water”), from aqua (“water”). Compare Romanian apătos.

nulât.etymology: nûl + -ât; compare also Italian nuvolato, Spanish and Portuguese nublado, Galician nubrado, Asturian nubláu; cf. Latin nūbilātus.

glosses_en: to become clouded, cloudy; cloud over
innulâsi.etymology: From in- + nûl + -â + si. Compare Catalan ennuvolar-se, Romanian (a se) înnora, Occitan ennivolar, compare also Venetan nuvołarse, Italian annuvolare, Portuguese nublar, Spanish nublar, anublar.

Udin.etymology: From Medieval Latin Utinum. Compare Italian Udine.

miscliçâ.etymology: Ultimately from Latin misceō (“mix”), through some derived form.

montagnôs.etymology: montagne + -ôs, or from Late Latin montāniōsus, from Latin montānus.

mulinâr.etymology: mulin + -âr, or from Late Latin molinārius, from molīnus, from Latin molō.

glosses_en: fee or renumeration for the grinding of grain (at a mill)
muldure.etymology: Probably from a Vulgar Latin *molitura, derived from Latin molō (“to grind”), through its past participle molitus. Compare French mouture (Old French molture), Spanish moltura, moldura (dialectal).

tont.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *tundus, back-derived from Late Latin retundus, from Latin rotundus.

glosses_en: small slice of some food (like salami)
rudiele.etymology: From Late Latin rotella, diminutive of Latin rota (“wheel”). Compare Italian rotella, Venetan rodèła, Portuguese rodela, etc.

umidî.etymology: From umid. Compare also Italian umidire, Romanian umezi.

signestri.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin sinextrum, from Latin sinistrum.

glosses_en: shrewd, astute, sagacious, clever, able, dexterous, crafty

sperance.etymology: sperâ + -ance, or from Vulgar Latin sperantia, from Latin sperans. Compare Italian speranza, French espérance.

coresime.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *quaresima, from Latin quadrāgēsima (“the fortieth part; Lent”), substantive of quadrāgēsimus (“fortieth”).

glosses_en: Lazio (an administrative region of Italy, situated in the central peninsular section of the country with Rome as its capital)

aradôr.etymology: From Latin arātōr, arātōrem. Equivalent to arâ + -dôr.

aradure.etymology: From Late Latin arātūra, from Latin arō. Equivalent to arâ + -dure.

lescje.etymology: From Latin ēsca, with the initial -l- probably appearing from its pairing with a preceding article. Compare Venetan lesca, Lombard lisca, Italian esca.

doncje.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin dunc, derived from Latin tunc + dum. Compare Ladin donca, Italian dunque, French donc.

stiçâ.etymology: From or related to stiç; compare Venetan stiçar, stisar. Perhaps linked to a Vulgar Latin *attitiō, attitiāre, from Latin titiō, and influenced by stiç, or from a variant root *extitiāre. Cf. also Italian attizzare.

glosses_en: castellan (lord or caretaker of a castle)
cjiscjelan.etymology: From Latin castellānus; equivalent to cjiscjel + -an. Compare Romansh chastellan, French châtelain.

cjapon.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin root *cappō, *cappōnem, from Latin cāpō. Compare Italian cappone, Venetan capón, French chapon.

cjiâ.etymology: From Latin cacāre. Compare French chier, Italian cacare.

cjamare.etymology: From Vulgar Latin camara, variant of Latin camera, from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára). Compare Venetan càmara, Italian camera, Romansh chambra, French chambre, Spanish cámara.

cjaviestri.etymology: From Latin capistrum. Compare French chevêtre, Italian capestro.

discuvierzi.etymology: From Late Latin discoperīre < discooperīre, from Latin dis- + cooperiō. By surface analysis, dis- + cuverizi.

discuviert.etymology: From Late Latin discoopertus, from Latin dis- + coopertus. Compare Italian discoperto, Venetan descoverto, French découvert.

cuviercli.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *coperclum, from Latin cooperculum. Compare Italian coperchio, French couvercle.

cuvierture.etymology: From Late Latin coopertūra, from Latin coopertus. Equivalent to cuviert + -ture. Compare Italian copertura, French couverture.

vuadagnâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *wadaniāre, of Germanic origin; from Frankish *waiþanjan (“to hunt, graze”) (a calque of Latin petere), from Proto-Germanic *waiþanjaną.

celâr.etymology: From Late Latin cellārium, from Latin cella.

cerviel.etymology: From Latin cerebellum, diminutive of cerebrum. Compare Italian cervello, French cerveau.

ciale.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin cicāla, from Latin cicāda.

cudumar.etymology: From Latin cucumis, cucumerem. Compare Occitan codombre, Romansh cucumer, Venetan cocomaro, cugumero, Italian cucumero.

suesar.etymology: From Latin socerus, variant of socer, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱuros.

gnocis.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *noptiās, from Latin nuptiās.

glosses_en: to thrust or drive; to put something into
ficjâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *fīg(i)cāre, frequentative based on Latin fīgere (“drive in, fix in place”).

ingjanâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin or Late Latin ingannāre (attested in a gloss), from Latin ganniō.

armadure.etymology: From Latin armātūra (“armour”). Equivalent to armâ + -dure.

pierdite.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *perdita, from the feminine of Latin perditus (“lost”), perfect passive participle of perdō (“to lose”).

cuaie.etymology: From Late Latin quaccola or an alternative form of it.

tortorele.etymology: From Late Latin turturella or Latin turturilla, from turtur. Compare French tourterelle, Romanian turturea, Italian tortorella.

radâ.etymology: Probably from Latin rādō, rādere, with a change of conjugation.

scae.etymology: Probably from Frankish *skallija (“scale, shell”), from Proto-Germanic *skaljō (“scale, shell, husk”) ( > English shell), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to cut, part, sunder, split, divide”). Compare Italian scaglia, Venetan scaja, Fr

porcarie.etymology: From a derivative of Latin porcus; related to purcit. Compare Italian porcheria, Venetan porcaria, Romanian porcărie, Portuguese porcaria, Spanish porquería.

glosses_en: layer, coat, coating, sheet, film, stratum

sivilâ.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *sīfilāre, probably an Osco-Umbrian influenced variant of Latin sībilāre. Compare Romansh tschivlar, schivlar, French siffler, Spanish chiflar.

'save.etymology: Borrowed from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *žaba.

-dure.etymology: From Latin -tūra. Compare Italian -tura, French -ure, Catalan -dura.

luvri.etymology: From Latin ūberem, accusative of ūber, with the initial -l- becoming attached from use with the indefinite pronoun il.

vidiele.etymology: From Late Latin vitella, diminutive of Latin vitula.

cussience.etymology: Ultimately from Latin cōnscientia. Compare Italian coscienza.

glosses_en: third-person singular present indicative of olsâ

noaltris.etymology: From Latin nos (“we”) + Latin alter (“other”). Akin to Spanish nosotros and Catalan nosaltres.

vualtris.etymology: From Latin vos (“ye”) + Latin alter (“other”). Akin to Spanish vosotros and Catalan vosaltres.
